--- title: "Logistic regression with a binary and numeric predictor" format: html: df-print: kable toc: true toc-depth: 3 number-sections: true --- # A continuous moderator In [logistic regression with two binary predictors](logistic-two-binary-predictors.qmd), baseline depression was grouped as below or at least 10 on the PHQ-9. That can be useful for a clearly defined clinical decision, but it also turns different scores into the same group. Here we retain the observed continuous `phq9_screen` score and ask: > How does the estimated probability of treatment response differ > between therapist-guided treatment and waitlist at different baseline PHQ-9 > scores? We will make that question concrete at PHQ-9 scores of 5, 10, and 15. They represent low, moderate, and higher values within the observed range; they are not diagnostic categories. Our primary result is a **therapist-guided minus waitlist probability difference**, expressed in percentage points with a 95% CI. A logistic-regression interaction is an interaction on the **log-odds scale**. That detail matters: even an additive logistic model can have probability differences that vary with PHQ-9, because the logit-to-probability transformation is nonlinear. We therefore calculate contrasts on the probability scale rather than reading their shape from a coefficient table. # Packages and analytic data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(here) library(marginaleffects) options( marginaleffects_print_omit = c("s.value"), marginaleffects_print_style = ifelse(interactive(), "summary", "tinytable") ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} df_binary <- read_csv2(here("data", "steps_clean.csv")) |> filter(!is.na(lsas_screen), !is.na(lsas_post)) |> mutate( # The second factor level is the event modelled by binomial glm(). lsas_response = factor( if_else((lsas_screen - lsas_post) / lsas_screen >= 0.30, "Response", "No response"), levels = c("No response", "Response") ), trt = factor( trt, levels = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided", "self-guided") ) ) |> filter(trt %in% c("waitlist", "therapist-guided")) |> drop_na(lsas_response, phq9_screen) |> droplevels() phq_values <- c(5, 10, 15) df_binary |> summarise( participants = n(), minimum_phq9 = min(phq9_screen), maximum_phq9 = max(phq9_screen) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| participants| minimum_phq9| maximum_phq9| |------------:|------------:|------------:| | 112| 1| 19|
::: ::: `Response` means a reduction of at least 30% from baseline LSAS. This is a response outcome, not a diagnostic or remission definition. Waitlist is the treatment reference group, and `Response` is the event whose probability is modelled. We restrict this chapter to the waitlist and therapist-guided arms so that every treatment contrast has one clear direction. # Additive logistic model ## What does “additive” mean here? The additive model has a treatment term and a PHQ-9 term, but no product term: $$ \operatorname{logit}\{P(Y_i = \text{Response} \mid trt_i, PHQ9_i)\} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\mathbf{1}\{trt_i = \text{therapist-guided}\} + \beta_2 PHQ9_i. $$ The therapist-guided versus waitlist **log-odds** difference is the same at every PHQ-9 score in this model. Equivalently, the treatment odds ratio is constant across PHQ-9. That is not the same as saying the probability difference is constant: a fixed change in log-odds maps to different probability changes near 0, 0.5, and 1. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_additive <- stats::glm( lsas_response ~ trt + phq9_screen, family = binomial, data = df_binary ) summary(mod_additive) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: stats::glm(formula = lsas_response ~ trt + phq9_screen, family = binomial, data = df_binary) Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) (Intercept) -1.68842 0.66201 -2.550 0.0108 * trttherapist-guided 2.42468 0.51322 4.724 2.31e-06 *** phq9_screen -0.04753 0.05270 -0.902 0.3671 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1) Null deviance: 142.11 on 111 degrees of freedom Residual deviance: 111.43 on 109 degrees of freedom AIC: 117.43 Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} additive_trt_difference <- avg_comparisons( mod_additive, variables = list(trt = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided")), type = "response" ) additive_trt_difference ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) 2.5 % 97.5 %
Type: response
0.461 0.0792 5.82 <0.001 0.306 0.616
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Model interpretation Averaged over the observed baseline PHQ-9 distribution, therapist-guided treatment is estimated to change the probability of a treatment response score by **46.1 percentage points** compared with waitlist (95% CI **30.6** to **61.6 percentage points**). This is therapist-guided minus waitlist; a positive value favours a higher estimated probability of response with therapist guidance. It is a population-average probability contrast over this analysis sample, conditional on the additive model—not a coefficient interpreted as a percentage-point change. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_predictions( mod_additive, by = c("phq9_screen", "trt"), type = "response" ) + labs( title = "Additive logistic model", subtitle = "Estimated probabilities with 95% confidence intervals", x = "Baseline PHQ-9 score", y = "Probability of treatment response", colour = "Treatment group", fill = "Treatment group" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Additive-model estimated probabilities of treatment response, with 95% confidence intervals.](logistic-binary-numeric-predictors_files/figure-html/plot-additive-probabilities-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The curves need not be parallel on the probability scale. The additive model makes its parallel-lines assumption on the log-odds scale, not on this plot's probability scale. # Interaction model ## Let the treatment association vary with PHQ-9 The interaction model adds a product term: $$ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{logit}\{P(Y_i = \text{Response} \mid trt_i, PHQ9_i)\} = &\ \beta_0 + \beta_1\mathbf{1}\{trt_i = \text{therapist-guided}\} + \\ &\ \beta_2 PHQ9_i + \beta_3\mathbf{1}\{trt_i = \text{therapist-guided}\} \times PHQ9_i. \end{aligned} $$ Now the treatment log-odds difference can change with PHQ-9. The treatment coefficient in `summary()` is the difference at PHQ-9 = 0, which is not a useful stand-alone clinical summary here. We instead estimate probability differences at prespecified, observed-range scores. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_interaction <- stats::glm( lsas_response ~ trt * phq9_screen, family = binomial, data = df_binary ) summary(mod_interaction) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: stats::glm(formula = lsas_response ~ trt * phq9_screen, family = binomial, data = df_binary) Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|) (Intercept) -1.81866 1.02038 -1.782 0.0747 . trttherapist-guided 2.60970 1.20900 2.159 0.0309 * phq9_screen -0.03400 0.09493 -0.358 0.7202 trttherapist-guided:phq9_screen -0.01944 0.11405 -0.170 0.8647 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 (Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1) Null deviance: 142.11 on 111 degrees of freedom Residual deviance: 111.40 on 108 degrees of freedom AIC: 119.4 Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} conditional_trt_difference <- avg_comparisons( mod_interaction, variables = list(trt = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided")), newdata = datagrid(phq9_screen = phq_values), by = "phq9_screen", type = "response" ) conditional_trt_difference ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
phq9_screen Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) 2.5 % 97.5 %
Type: response
5 0.508 0.1120 4.53 < 0.001 0.288 0.727
10 0.460 0.0799 5.76 < 0.001 0.304 0.617
15 0.409 0.1258 3.25 0.00116 0.162 0.655
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Model interpretation At PHQ-9 = 5, therapist-guided minus waitlist is an estimated **50.8 percentage-point** difference in the probability of treatment response (95% CI **28.8** to **72.7**). At PHQ-9 = 10, the corresponding difference is **46.0 percentage points** (95% CI **30.4** to **61.7**); at PHQ-9 = 15 it is **40.9 percentage points** (95% CI **16.2** to **65.5**). Each contrast conditions on the displayed PHQ-9 value. Positive values mean a higher modelled probability with therapist-guided treatment. The estimates and intervals, rather than the interaction coefficient alone, describe whether the clinically relevant probability difference changes across PHQ-9. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_predictions( mod_interaction, by = c("phq9_screen", "trt"), type = "response" ) + labs( title = "Interaction logistic model", subtitle = "Estimated probabilities with 95% confidence intervals", x = "Baseline PHQ-9 score", y = "Probability of treatment response", colour = "Treatment group", fill = "Treatment group" ) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Interaction-model estimated probabilities of treatment response, with 95% confidence intervals.](logistic-binary-numeric-predictors_files/figure-html/plot-interaction-probabilities-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ## A curve of the conditional probability difference The probability curves are useful, but they leave the reader to visually subtract two uncertain quantities. A direct contrast plot answers the treatment question more directly. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot_comparisons( mod_interaction, variables = list(trt = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided")), condition = "phq9_screen", type = "response" ) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") + labs( title = "Conditional treatment probability difference", subtitle = "Therapist-guided minus waitlist; 95% confidence intervals", x = "Baseline PHQ-9 score", y = "Probability difference" ) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1)) + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Conditional therapist-guided-minus-waitlist probability difference across baseline PHQ-9, with 95% confidence intervals.](logistic-binary-numeric-predictors_files/figure-html/plot-conditional-treatment-difference-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The dashed zero line marks no modelled probability difference. Wide intervals at the edge of the observed PHQ-9 range are a reminder not to make subgroup claims from the curve's point estimates alone. # Conditional and population-average treatment contrasts A conditional contrast answers a question such as “what is the modelled difference at PHQ-9 = 10?” A population-average contrast answers a different question: “what is the modelled treatment difference after averaging each participant's counterfactual predictions over the observed PHQ-9 distribution?” ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} marginal_trt_difference <- avg_comparisons( mod_interaction, variables = list(trt = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided")), type = "response" ) marginal_trt_difference ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
Estimate Std. Error z Pr(>|z|) 2.5 % 97.5 %
Type: response
0.461 0.079 5.83 <0.001 0.306 0.616
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Model interpretation Averaged over the observed PHQ-9 distribution, the interaction model estimates that therapist-guided treatment changes the probability of a low post-treatment LSAS score by **46.1 percentage points** compared with waitlist (95% CI **30.6** to **61.6 percentage points**). This population-average contrast is not the effect at a particular PHQ-9 score. It averages conditional contrasts over the PHQ-9 values represented in this sample, so it can change if the target population's baseline PHQ-9 distribution changes. ::: # Odds ratios are not probability differences The exponentiated treatment coefficient from the interaction model is an odds ratio **at PHQ-9 = 0**. That value is outside the useful interpretive range for this example, so reporting it alone would be particularly misleading. To see how the odds ratio changes with PHQ-9 in the interaction model, we can estimate the treatment log-odds difference at the same three values and exponentiate it. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} conditional_trt_log_odds <- avg_comparisons( mod_interaction, variables = list(trt = c("waitlist", "therapist-guided")), newdata = datagrid(phq9_screen = phq_values), by = "phq9_screen", type = "link" ) |> transmute( phq9_screen, odds_ratio = exp(estimate), conf.low = exp(conf.low), conf.high = exp(conf.high) ) conditional_trt_log_odds ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
2.5 % 97.5 %
2.93 52.0
4.08 30.7
2.11 48.9
``` ::: ::: An odds ratio compares odds, $p/(1-p)$, rather than probabilities. For example, an odds ratio of 2 means that the modelled odds are twice as large; it does not mean that the probability rises by 100 percentage points or necessarily doubles. The probability change depends on the starting probability. For the clinical question in this chapter, report the conditional probability differences and their CIs first; use the odds ratios to read and critique the statistical literature accurately. # Summary - An additive logistic model assumes a common treatment **log-odds** difference, not necessarily a constant probability difference. - An interaction model lets the treatment association vary with continuous baseline PHQ-9. - `avg_comparisons(..., type = "response")` supplies conditional and population-average treatment contrasts on the probability scale. - A contrast curve communicates both the estimated pattern and its uncertainty. - Odds ratios describe ratios of odds. They are not percentage-point changes in probability.
